title: Metacognitive Awareness and EFL Learners' Perceptions and Experiences in Utilising ChatGPT for Writing Feedback
extended_summary:
This paper examines how EFL learners perceive and experience using ChatGPT for writing feedback, with a particular focus on the role of metacognitive awareness. The study asks three main questions: how ChatGPT influences students' writing experiences and metacognitive awareness, how differences in metacognitive awareness relate to students' perceptions and practices, and what factors shape effective use of ChatGPT for writing support. The paper is not about secondary school settings; it studies university-level learners in an English practical writing course.

The intervention involved one class using AI tools during a semester-long process-oriented writing course while another class followed a teacher-led, peer-collaboration approach without AI. Because ChatGPT was unavailable in Macau, the AI group used Poe to access ChatGPT for free classroom use. The AI-supported class used the tool for writing tasks and feedback during class. Data came from questionnaires on writing motivation, engagement, self-efficacy, collaborative writing tendency, and metacognitive awareness, as well as semi-structured interviews with students with high and low metacognitive awareness.

Participants were 40 EFL undergraduates in two English Practical Writing classes at a single institution in Macau, taught by the same instructor over 15 weeks. Students were randomly divided so that one class used AI tools and the other did not, although the report frames the overall work as a mixed-methods study combining quantitative group comparisons, regression analyses, and qualitative thematic analysis. The context was an authentic classroom course rather than a laboratory task.

The study concludes that AI-supported writing was associated with significantly higher post-test scores on motivation for writing, collaborative writing tendency, writing engagement, and multiple aspects of metacognitive awareness, with weaker evidence for self-efficacy. Interview findings suggest that effective use of ChatGPT-like feedback depended on metacognitive awareness, critical thinking, and cognitive effort. Students with higher metacognitive awareness were more likely to evaluate, monitor, and refine AI feedback rather than copy it directly, whereas lower-awareness students were more likely to accept outputs uncritically or disengage. The paper also notes concerns around over-reliance and ethical use, but it does not provide detailed operational reporting on prompt design, feedback cycle structure, plagiarism safeguards, privacy routines, or fidelity tracking.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a semester-long mixed-method comparative study with a control group (AI vs non-AI) and pre/post measurement, which is stronger than simple correlational work. However, it is not a K-12 study, randomization appears at class level with a very small sample (n=40), and outcomes are primarily self-report rather than direct writing-performance measures, so important credibility concerns remain.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant, generally favorable differences for the AI group across multiple writing-related and metacognitive outcomes, with mean differences that appear practically meaningful, but no standardized effect sizes are reported. Impact is therefore best classified as modest-to-promising rather than clearly large.

interventions.use_case: EFL undergraduates used Poe/ChatGPT as a writing feedback and assistance tool during a semester-long practical writing course to obtain feedback on drafts, support revision, and guide planning/monitoring/evaluation of writing.
Students interacted conversationally with Poe as an alternative interface to ChatGPT for feedback-seeking, prompt-based writing support, and iterative dialogue about their writing.

finding.finding_summary: In a 15-week EFL writing course with 40 undergraduates (AI group n=20; non-AI group n=20), the AI group showed significantly higher post-test writing-related outcomes than the comparison group on measures tied to writing experience and perceived writing support. Post-test means favored AI use for motivation for writing (4.34 vs. 3.59, p<0.001), collaborative writing tendency (4.14 vs. 3.58, p<0.001), and writing engagement (4.26 vs. 3.48, p<0.001), with self-efficacy also higher (3.96 vs. 3.66, p=0.037); however, no standardized writing-quality effect size on actual draft performance was reported.
finding.measure: Questionnaire-based writing perceptions/experiences in EFL writing course (motivation, self-efficacy, collaborative writing tendency, engagement)
finding.std_deviation: Reported for post-test subscales: MW AI 0.38 vs control 0.35; SEW 0.52 vs 0.34; CBW 0.45 vs 0.37; WE 0.54 vs 0.39

finding.finding_summary: The AI-supported group reported significantly better social-emotional writing outcomes after the course than the non-AI group, especially for motivation and engagement. Mann-Whitney results on gain scores favored the AI group for motivation for writing (p<0.0001), collaborative writing tendency (p=0.0024), and writing engagement (p=0.0002), while self-efficacy gains were only marginally significant (p=0.064; t-test p=0.056).
finding.measure: Self-report Likert scales for motivation for writing, engagement, self-efficacy, and collaborative writing tendency
finding.std_deviation: Gain-score SDs reported in t-test table: MW 1.17 AI vs 0.36 control; SEW 0.60 AI vs 0.37 control; CBW 0.51 AI vs 0.45 control; WE 0.75 AI vs 0.46 control

finding.finding_summary: The study found substantial positive associations between ChatGPT-supported writing and metacognitive awareness. On post-test measures, the AI group outperformed the non-AI group across declarative knowledge (4.40 vs. 3.46, p<0.001), procedural knowledge (4.09 vs. 3.54, p<0.001), conditional knowledge (4.26 vs. 3.44, p<0.001), planning (4.14 vs. 3.64, p<0.001), monitoring (3.97 vs. 3.40, p<0.001), and evaluating (4.22 vs. 3.50, p<0.001). Regression further showed metacognitive awareness strongly predicted perceptions/experiences using ChatGPT (coefficient=1.23980, p<0.001; model R²=0.8631).
finding.measure: Metacognitive Writing Strategies Questionnaire and regression linking metacognitive awareness to ChatGPT-related perceptions/practices
finding.std_deviation: Post-test SDs reported: DK 0.27 AI vs 0.32 control; PK 0.47 vs 0.38; CK 0.36 vs 0.36; Planning 0.31 vs 0.27; Monitoring 0.28 vs 0.19; Evaluating 0.22 vs 0.18
